text: Donald Clarence Simpson (October 29, 1943 – January 19, 1996) was an American film producer, screenwriter, and actor renowned for his work on major blockbuster films of the 1980s and 1990s. He began his career in the 1970s at Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures, where he worked in marketing exploitation films, including Woodstock and A Clockwork Orange, and co-wrote and had a small role in the 1976 film Cannonball. In 1975, he was interviewed for a position at Paramount by his friend Steve Tisch, who declined the offer, and was later named vice-president of production in 1977 and president in 1981. He was fired in 1982 after passing out during a studio meeting due to drug use and was known for managing eight productions simultaneously and frequently throwing tantrums during filming. He formed a professional partnership with Jerry Bruckheimer, producing successful films such as Flashdance (1983), Beverly Hills Cop (1984), Top Gun (1986), Beverly Hills Cop II (1987), and The Rock (1996), the latter released posthumously. The duo earned Producers of the Year honors from the National Association of Theatre Owners in 1985 and 1988 and launched their own production company affiliated with Paramount in 1985. In 1990, they signed a five-year $300 million deal with Paramount, which ended after Days of Thunder (1990) underperformed at the box office despite a $60 million budget and grossing $158 million, with both parties blaming each other for the results. They later signed with Disney, with The Ref (1994) being a financial failure, but returned to success with Dangerous Minds, Crimson Tide, and Bad Boys in 1995. Simpson never married; he took Scientology classes in the 1970s but quit after spending $25,000 with no personal gains, and during Days of Thunder, he expelled Scientology leader David Miscavige after refusing to pay for a costly sound device. Known for his brash personality, Simpson made controversial remarks, such as criticizing Steven Spielberg and David Lynch, and claimed his primary duty as a producer was to make money. He worked out daily with equipment provided by Arnold Schwarzenegger and frequented Canyon Ranch for workouts and tanning. Though he claimed never to have had plastic surgery, reports indicate he underwent ten procedures between 1988 and 1994, including a penis-enlargement surgery, which led to infections and reversals. Simpson was infamous for his extravagant lifestyle, often describing making movies as the best thing after eating and having sex, and was a central figure in Hollywood's cocaine-party scene, hosting lavish all-night parties and being known for S&M preferences. He used cocaine since the 1970s, increasing his use over time, and was known for erratic behavior and excessive spending. In a 1994 interview, he claimed to have stopped using drugs and only had a food addiction, but screenwriter James Toback stated his drug use never ceased, prompting David Geffen and Jeffrey Katzenberg to intervene. Simpson refused traditional rehab and instead worked with doctor Stephen Ammerman, who developed a "dangerously unorthodox" detox program involving medications like morphine to manage withdrawal. Ammerman died in August 1995 at Simpson’s home from an accidental overdose of cocaine, Valium, venlafaxine, and morphine. Frustrated by Simpson’s drug use and declining performance, Bruckheimer ended their partnership in December 1995, agreeing to complete The Rock, which was dedicated to Simpson’s memory. Simpson died on January 19, 1996, in the bathroom of his Bel Air, Los Angeles, home, initially attributed to natural causes; an autopsy revealed he died of heart failure from combined drug intoxication, with 21 different drugs detected in his system, including antidepressants, stimulants, sedatives, and tranquilizers. Investigations revealed he obtained prescription drugs from 15 doctors, with 2,200 pills found in his bedroom closet, and his monthly prescription expenses totaled over $60,000. A 1998 book by Charles Fleming described him as "a supercharged simple-minded creature, an Aesop's fable on crystal meth." After his death, his brother Lary Simpson established a production banner to develop projects originated by Don Simpson, which continued until Lary’s death on January 25, 2023, at age 77. Simpson is credited as a producer on all films unless otherwise noted.
